newsitem.title: USA: Fabri-Centers pays $3.28 million to settle SEC charges.
newsitem.headline: Fabri-Centers pays $3.28 million to settle SEC charges.

text.p: Fabri-Centres of America Inc., a nationwide fabrics retailer, has agreed to repay $3.28 million in illegal proceeds it received after inflating its earnings, federal securities regulators said Tuesday.

The proceeds were from a March 1992 sale of $74.75 million in convertible debt from which the Securities and Exchange Commission said the company yielded a better price and more favourable terms than it otherwise would have because investors were misled by its overstated earnings.

In a settlement that was disclosed simultaneously with the filing of a civil complaint by the SEC in U.S. District Court in Washington, the company also accepted a court order barring it from further violations of securities laws, although it did not admit or deny the charges, the agency said.

Fabri-Centres, a Hudson, Ohio-based operator of 915 retail fabric and crafts stores, and two of its former executives overstated the company's earnings and profitability in public documents for the fiscal year ended Feb. 1, 1992, the SEC said.

In the public documents, the company deviated from its prior accounting practice, misused the "gross profit method" of accounting, erroneously calculated a key inventory reserve and failed to disclose to its shareholders that it was engaged in heightened price competition, the agency said.
The company's March 1992 convertible debt offering would have been less lucrative for if it had provided accurate information, the SEC said.
The company does business under the names Jo-Ann Fabrics and Crafts, Cloth World and New York Fabrics and Crafts.

The two former officers, former Chief Financial Officer Robert Norton, and former Comptroller Joseph Williams, did not agree to settle charges that they circumvented the company's internal accounting controls and that Norton made false and misleading statements to auditors about the offering, it said.
The SEC said it is moving ahead with civil litigation against them before U.S. District Court Judge Harold Greene.

Norton's lawyers, Stanley Arkin and John Sturc, issued a statement calling the complaint an "unjustified dispute over the application of accounting principles" and said the SEC could not present evidence that he commited any violations.

"Rather, the evidence will show that Norton and his subordinates carefully applied the correct accounting principles and caused Fabri-Centres to make prompt and accurate disclosures," the attorneys said.

Charges against the company also include making material false public statements in May and June 1992, violating anti-fraud provisions of federal securities laws and violating reporting, record-keeping and internal controls provisions.
The SEC said it also simultaneously brought and settled administrative allegations against Alan Rosskamm, the current chairman and chief executive of Fabri-Centres.

Without admitting or denying the charges, the agency said Hudson consented to findings that he violated securities laws by failing to make adequate inquiries before signing off on letters to the company's independent auditors and by signing and approving company documents filed with the SEC.
